name: Havana
info: Havana is the capital and largest city of Cuba, on the island’s northern coast, settled by the Spanish at its present site in 1519 and long a treasure-fleet port, a fortress city, a slave-trade port and a republican capital.

facts.founded: Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar founded San Cristóbal de la Habana in 1514 on the south coast of Cuba; that settlement failed, and the town that became Havana grew at its present site beside Puerto de Carenas in 1519.
facts.where: On the northern coast of Cuba along the Straits of Florida, around a bay entered through a narrow inlet, with the Almendares River crossing the city from south to north.
facts.known: A harbour on the Gulf Stream; the assembly point of the Spanish treasure fleet; forts and walls; the shipyard of El Arsenal; the British siege of 1762; the slave trade and sugar; the capital of the Republic of Cuba from 1902; the revolution of 1959
facts.today: Havana is the capital and largest city of Cuba and is both a city and a province, with Old Havana on UNESCO’s World Heritage list.

t: The Spanish moved Havana to its present harbour in 1519, and from 1561 the ships bound for Spain were required to gather in its bay, which made it the main port of Spain’s American colonies.
Pirate attacks, beginning with the burning of 1555, led the Crown to fortify the city, and after the British siege of 1762 the Spanish made it the most heavily fortified city in the Americas.

Sugar and the slave trade brought riches to the city, slavery stayed legal in Cuba until 1886, and Havana became the capital of the independent Republic of Cuba in 1902 and the seat of the revolutionary government after 1959.
dyk: In 1763 Britain gave Havana back to Spain in return for Florida, less than a year after taking the city, and more than half of the British force that took it died, mostly of illness and in particular yellow fever.
ev: The town that became Havana is settled beside Puerto de Carenas, on the north coast
The French corsair Jacques de Sores takes Havana and burns much of it
A royal decree requires all ships bound for Spain to assemble in Havana Bay
Philip II of Spain grants Havana the title of city
A British fleet and army besiege and take Havana, which Spain recovers in 1763
The first railway in Cuba opens between Havana and Bejucal
Spain relinquishes sovereignty over Cuba after the sinking of the USS Maine in Havana harbour
The Cuban Revolution brings Fidel Castro’s government to power in Havana

sections.origins:
Havana lies on the northern coast of Cuba along the Straits of Florida, south of the Florida Keys, where the Gulf of Mexico joins the Atlantic Ocean. Sebastián de Ocampo’s circumnavigation of the island in 1508 brought the first Spaniards to the place, and in 1510 the first Spanish colonists arrived from Hispaniola and began the conquest of Cuba. In 1514 Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar founded San Cristóbal de la Habana on the south coast, and an early map of 1514 places it at the mouth of the Mayabeque River. That settlement failed, mainly because the land around the river was low and swampy, and every Spanish attempt to found a town on that coast failed.

Between 1514 and 1519 the Spanish made settlements on the north coast. One of them, La Chorrera, stood beside the mouth of the Almendares River on higher and less marshy ground, and later became the neighbourhoods of Vedado and Miramar. The town that became Havana grew in 1519 next to what was then called Puerto de Carenas, ‘Careening Port’, and the quality of the harbour led to the change of site. Bartolomé de las Casas wrote that ships had been careened there, which gave the port its name. Pánfilo de Narváez gave the town, the sixth founded in Cuba, the name San Cristóbal de la Habana. San Cristóbal is its patron saint, and Habana may come from Habaguanex, the chief of a local Taíno-speaking people about whom little else is known.
sections.growth:
The harbour lay at the entrance to the Gulf of Mexico, with easy access to the Gulf Stream that navigators followed from the Americas to Europe, and this led to its early growth as the principal port of Spain’s colonies in the New World. After the French attack of 1555 the Crown paid for fortresses to guard the main cities and to tighten its control of trade. A royal decree of 1561 then required every ship bound for Spain to assemble in Havana Bay. Ships arrived from May to August, waited for the best weather, and left together by September. Gold, silver, emeralds, mahogany, leather, spices, corn, manioc and cocoa passed through the port, and the gathered ships needed food, water and other goods from the city’s farms and workshops. In 1563 the captain general moved his residence from Santiago de Cuba to Havana.

On 20 December 1592 Philip II granted Havana the title of city, and the Crown later named it ‘Key to the New World and Rampart of the West Indies’. The city expanded greatly in the 17th century, building mostly in wood. By the middle of the 18th century it had more than seventy thousand inhabitants and was the third-largest city in the Americas, behind Lima and Mexico City and ahead of Boston and New York. By 1740 it had Spain’s largest and most active shipyard and the only drydock in the New World, and El Arsenal built 109 ships, among them the Santísima Trinidad, launched in 1769. The railway of 1837 carried sugar from the Güines valley to the harbour. Sugar and a flourishing slave trade first brought riches to the city.
sections.rulers:
Havana was a town of the Spanish colony of Cuba, and its city council was created in 1550 under the Governorate of Cuba. The governor’s residence moved there in 1563, and the Captaincy General of Cuba, with its council, lasted from 1607 to 1898. In 1762 a British fleet and army took the city, which Sir George Keppel governed for Britain until the Treaty of Paris of 1763 returned it to Spain in exchange for Florida. Spain then rebuilt its defences. In 1796 the remains of Christopher Columbus were brought to Havana from Santo Domingo, and they stayed until 1898.

The war of Cuban independence from Spain had been under way for three years when the USS Maine sank in Havana harbour, and on 12 August 1898, in the Spanish–American War, Spain relinquished sovereignty over Cuba. The island was then occupied by the United States. Cuba adopted a constitution in 1901, and in 1902 Havana became the capital of the new Republic of Cuba, with Tomás Estrada Palma as its first president. In July 1940 it hosted the Havana Conference, at which the United States and 20 Latin American countries agreed to defend European colonies in the Americas if their home countries fell to the Axis.

After the revolution of 1959 the municipal government was restructured with the rest of the state. The constitution of 1976 gave Havana the status of both a city and a province, and in 2010 the former province of La Habana was divided into Artemisa and Mayabeque.
sections.life:
The Taíno population of Cuba was virtually wiped out by Eurasian diseases in the earliest period of the Spanish conquest. Havana’s settlers were Spaniards, and Cuba received millions of immigrants during the Republic; it is estimated that one quarter of the Cuban population descends from Spanish immigrants. Sugar and a flourishing slave trade first brought riches to the city. In 1557 the city council banned freed black men from owning taverns or inns and from selling tobacco or wine. Slavery stayed legal in Cuba until 1886. Chinese labourers, mostly Cantonese, were brought in the mid-19th century on work contracts of eight years, and many stayed. After the American Civil War ended in 1865 former Confederates, among them the Confederate secretary of state Judah P. Benjamin, came to Havana, and some former slaveholders went on running plantations there. The census of 2012 recorded 58.4% of the city’s people as white, 26.4% as mixed, 15.2% as black and 0.2% as Asian.

Roman Catholics form the largest religious group, and the cathedral, built from 1748 and completed in 1777, is dedicated to San Cristóbal. Before 1959 the Jewish community numbered more than 15,000, many of them refugees from Nazi persecution, and many left for Miami or Israel after 1959. The University of Havana was established in 1728, and the Gran Teatro opened in 1837. The city made rum, cigars and ships, and the walls built from 1674 to 1740 were knocked down in 1863 so that it could grow.
sections.crises:
The first attack on Havana was by the French corsair Jacques de Sores in 1555, who took the city easily, plundered it and burned much of it, leaving without the great wealth he had hoped for. In 1649 an epidemic brought from Cartagena in Colombia affected a third of the population. A hurricane in 1730 destroyed the women’s hospital and the church of San Francisco de Paula, which were rebuilt and enlarged in 1745.

The British siege began on 6 June 1762, when more than 50 ships and over 11,000 men landed east of the city. The British took the heights of La Punta and bombarded El Morro Castle and the city. El Morro fell on 30 July, after the death of its defender Luis Vicente de Velasco e Isla, and the city surrendered on 13 August. The British lost 560 men to combat wounds, but more than half of their force ultimately died of illness, yellow fever in particular. In 1898 the sinking of the USS Maine in the harbour was the immediate cause of the Spanish–American War.

After 1959 all private property and industry were expropriated, and by 1966 to 1968 all privately owned businesses had been nationalised. The United States imposed an embargo, and shortages hit Cuba and Havana hard. When the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991 its subsidies to Cuba ended, and a severe downturn followed in the 1990s, known as the Special Period. Many buildings decayed, and partial or total collapses have injured and killed people. A tornado in January 2019 killed eight people and injured 195, and in 2022 at least 40 people died in an explosion at the Hotel Saratoga.
sections.legacy:
Old Havana was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982. Its forts, among them El Morro, built between 1589 and 1630, San Salvador de la Punta, the Real Fuerza and San Carlos de la Cabaña, which the Spanish began after 1763, record the years when the city guarded the route of the treasure fleet. The cathedral, built from 1748 to 1777, is the best example of Cuban Baroque. The Capitolio of 1929 and the Necrópolis Cristóbal Colón, built in 1876 and holding nearly a million tombs, belong to later periods, and Jean-Claude Nicolas Forestier, head of urban planning in Paris, worked on the city’s master plan from 1925, though the Great Depression cut short many of his ideas.

The coat of arms shows the three castles of the city, the Fuerza, the Morro and the Punta, with a key for the gateway to the New World, the title the Crown gave it. Contemporary Havana is three cities in one: Old Havana, Vedado and the newer suburban districts. The city reached 1 million inhabitants in the 1943 census, and its population was 2,142,939 in 2021 and 1,749,964 by the end of 2024. It is the capital and largest city of Cuba and the seat of its government, and it has 15 municipalities and 105 people’s councils.

summary: Havana was founded on the south coast of Cuba in 1514 and settled at its present harbour in 1519. It became the assembly point of the Spanish treasure fleet, a fortress city taken by Britain in 1762, a port of the slave trade and, from 1902, the capital of Cuba.
references: Alicia García Santana, Havana: History and Architecture of a Romantic City (Monacelli, 2000)
notes: FOUNDING: the articles give 1514 (Velázquez, south coast, failed) and 1519 (the present site). I used start 1519 and gave 1514 in facts and the origins section.

CAPITAL STATUS: the main article says Havana became capital of the island in 1552; the history article says the governor moved there in 1563, which 'unofficially sanctioned' its status. The two disagree, so I left 1552 out and used 1563 only as the governor's move.
RAILWAY: the main article says Cuba was the seventh country with a railway; the history article says fifth. Left out. The 1837 railway itself is in both.
1649 EPIDEMIC: the main article says yellow fever that killed a third; the history article says a fatal epidemic that affected a third. I wrote 'affected a third'.
EMBARGO: the main article gives 1960 in History and 1961 in Tourism for the US embargo. I gave no year.
TORNADO: the main article gives the night of 27 January and the evening of 28 January 2019, and 'over 190' and 195 injured. I wrote 'January 2019', eight killed, 195 injured (the Geography figure).

SAN CARLOS DE LA CABAÑA: the history article calls it the biggest Spanish fortification in the New World, the main article the third biggest; I gave no ranking. The main article also dates it 1558 to 1577, which contradicts 'begun after 1763'; I used only the history article's account of the work begun after 1763.

THE SLAVE TRADE: neither article gives numbers, dates of arrival or conditions. They say only that sugar and a flourishing slave trade first brought riches to the city, that slavery was legal in Cuba until 1886 and the council's 1557 ban on freed black men. I stated nothing further. 'The enslaved people brought through the port' is an inference from the slave trade; the editor may wish to check the wording.
Chinese contract labourers: the article's figure of over 200,000 before the revolution was left out as doubtful.

CHRONOLOGY: the history article says Cortés organised his Mexican expedition from the island; left out for space. The 'Paris of the Antilles' and Republican-era tourism, casinos, organised crime and the Hemingway quotation were left out as outside the brief. Post-1959 political and economic judgements ('dilapidated', 'failed to generate revenue') were left out.

SPANISH-AMERICAN WAR: 'Spain relinquished sovereignty on 12 August 1898' is from the main article; 'occupied by the United States' is from the history article ('the 20th century began with Havana ... under occupation by the USA').
POPULATION: the 2021 and end of 2024 figures are the article's official figures, given without 'as of'. The 1943 census 'agglomeration reached 1 million' is as given.

The Spanish–American War in the article is called the cause of Spain's loss; the claim in the rulers section that independence was 'fought for' is from the main article's note of the war of independence underway for three years. The 12 August date and the claim that the Maine was the 'immediate cause' are the article's wording.
FORESTIER: the main article says 'Jean-Claude Nicolas Forestier, the head of urban planning in Paris moved to Havana for five years' from 1925; I wrote worked on the plan from 1925.
